title: Module Two From Nothing: the Procedure
lead: Six steps that answer any Module Two question, including one you have never seen, without knowing the topic in advance: read the ask, mark the scenario, run the artefact's recipe, validate, and write the habits that carry marks.
intro:
Module Two is the one module where a procedure genuinely substitutes for knowledge. Every question asks for an artefact, and every artefact has a numbered recipe the course text prints. Learn the recipes and the routing, and an unseen scenario is just new nouns.

How to use this page

Read it once tonight, then work the questions in Past Questions: Module Two with it open beside you. In the hall, run the six steps in order and do not improvise.

extraBlocks.text: Step 0: read the ask, not the story

extraBlocks.label: Where the marks are decided
extraBlocks.html:
Find the imperative verbs: draw, identify, list, explain, state, read, outline. The story is raw material; the ask names the artefact, and the artefact decides everything you do next.

Write the marks beside each part before you start. The conversion is reliable: one mark is one labelled item or one sentence. A 4.5 mark ERD wants roughly four or five labelled things, not a page of prose.

extraBlocks.label: Mark the question paper itself
extraBlocks.tag: this alone answers most of the drawing marks
extraBlocks.html:
1. Underline every noun the system keeps data about. Those become entities, data stores or classes. Someone who only hands something in is an external agent, not an entity.
  2. Underline every verb an actor performs. Those become processes, use cases or relationship names.
  3. Circle every counting phrase: one, many, one of many, only one, at least, may or may not, over time. Those are your cardinality and ordinality, and they are the examiner's own words, so quote them back.
  4. Mark who is inside and who is outside. Anyone whose work the system records is inside it; anyone who submits or receives is outside.

None of that needs you to know the topic. It needs you to read carefully, which is the skill this module actually tests.

extraBlocks.label: 3A. ERD, five steps
extraBlocks.tag: four sightings across the two papers
extraBlocks.html:
1. Entities. One rectangle per underlined noun, named with a SINGULAR noun. Test it: does it have more than one instance? If not, it is not an entity.
  2. Attributes. Three or four per entity as ovals, joined to it by a line, with the identifier marked. Add the line that earns its own mark: an identifier should never be blank and never need to change.
  3. Relationships. A diamond between two entities, named with an ACTIVE VERB, so the diagram reads as a sentence: Customer Places Order.
  4. Cardinality, asking each direction separately. "Can one customer place many orders? Yes. Can one order belong to many customers? No." That is 1:M. Yes and yes is M:N, and a many to many needs an associative entity to hold whatever belongs to the pairing.
  5. Ordinality. Optional is a minimum of zero, mandatory a minimum of one. Cardinality is the maximum, ordinality the minimum. State both for every line, and name your notation: this course text draws Chen, diamonds and ovals.

extraBlocks.label: 3B. DFD, three levels in order
extraBlocks.tag: and the sentence that earns a mark in ten seconds
extraBlocks.html:
1. Context diagram. One rounded box numbered 0, the whole system, external agents around it, only the flows that cross the boundary, and no data stores.
  2. Level 0. The major processes numbered 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, plus the data stores. Exactly one Level 0 exists per system, which is asked directly.
  3. Level 1. Explodes ONE process into 1.1, 1.2, 1.3. Only the one the question names.
  4. The balancing sentence: "the flows into and out of process 3.0 are conserved by 3.1 to 3.3, so the diagrams balance."

Naming, which carries its own marks: agents are singular nouns, flows are nouns, processes are VERBS and never procedural ("Increment counter", not "Add 1 to the counter"), stores are nouns with no verbs.

extraBlocks.label: 3C. Use case diagram, four steps
extraBlocks.html:
1. Actors, named with nouns, found by five questions: who provides input, who receives output, are interfaces to other systems needed, is anything triggered automatically at a set time, who maintains the information. If payment or notification is mentioned, that outside party is an actor too.
  2. Use cases, one oval per verb phrase an actor performs.
  3. The boundary, a labelled rectangle with every oval inside it and every actor outside. An undrawn boundary loses marks on its own.
  4. Include and extend. Happens every time is an include; happens only under a condition is an extend, and its arrow points FROM the extension TO the base. Both are dashed, so the label and the direction are all you have.

If a narrative is also asked, its seven parts are: name and identifier, actors, description and goal, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions. The alternative flows are the part most answers drop and the reason the technique exists.

extraBlocks.label: 3D, 3E and 3F. Reading back, requirements, and theory lists
extraBlocks.html:
3D. Read a diagram back. Read every line TWICE, once in each direction: "one Customer places many Orders", then "each Order is placed by exactly one Customer". That is the whole answer to any read and interpret question.

3E. Requirements. Per technique, four clauses: who you would use it on, what it collects, why it suits this project, one limitation. The seven techniques: sampling existing documentation, research and site visits, observation, questionnaires, interviews, prototyping, JRP. Choose by cost to the user: documents cost nothing, questionnaires reach many cheaply, interviews are expensive, and observation is the only one that reveals the workaround nobody mentions.

The categories, one line each: business what the organisation wants, user what a person can do, functional what the system does, non functional how well it does it, system what it must run on or integrate with.

3F. Theory lists. Name the list, then tie one clause of it to the scenario in front of you. A list with no scenario earns the definition mark and nothing else.

extraBlocks.text: Step 4: the two minute validation pass

extraBlocks.label: Run this before you hand anything in
extraBlocks.tag: every line is a mark somebody loses
extraBlocks.html:
• Every data flow touches a process. No store to store, agent to agent, or store to agent.
  • No black hole (in, no out), miracle (out, no in) or gray hole (inputs too thin for the outputs).
  • Entities are singular; processes are verbs; stores carry no verbs.
  • Every relationship has a verb name and cardinality in both directions, with ordinality stated.
  • Boundary drawn, actors outside, include and extend labelled and pointing the right way.
  • The balancing sentence is written under the levelled DFD.

extraBlocks.text: Step 5: the four habits that earn marks without knowledge

extraBlocks.label: Write it the way it is marked
extraBlocks.html:
1. Write the recipe's step names as headings and answer under each. The course text numbers every procedure, and an examiner marking to a scheme is looking for those steps.
  2. Quote the scenario's own phrase beside each decision: "a truck may or may not be carrying stock, so participation is optional".
  3. State any assumption rather than hiding it: "the colour depth is not given, so 24 bits is assumed".
  4. Name your notation, and if the paper asks for another one, draw the fork on the many end and keep the same reasoning.

methodFrames.teach: The routing is the only part you must do from memory, so drill it here. Every question below is one you have actually been set.
methodFrames.ask: "Draw an ERD to model the relationships between the identified entities." Which recipe, and what is your first move?

methodFrames.check: The ERD recipe. First move: underline every noun the system keeps data about.
methodFrames.teach: That is 2025/2026 Question One (a). The nouns are the landlord, the house, the agent, the supervisor and the payment, and the supervisor is the tenant, which the wording hides.
methodFrames.ask: "Draw a Context diagram to model the entire system." What goes on it, and what must NOT?

methodFrames.check: One process numbered 0, the external agents, and the flows across the boundary. No data stores.
methodFrames.teach: 2025/2026 Question One (b)(i). The commonest error is drawing stores on a context diagram, and the second commonest is numbering the process 1 instead of 0.
methodFrames.ask: "Read and interpret the following ERD by providing the cardinal relationships between the entities." What do you write?

methodFrames.check: Each line as two sentences, one in each direction.
methodFrames.teach: 2024/2025 Question Three (c). One Customer places many Orders; each Order is placed by exactly one Customer. Two sentences per line, and nothing else is needed.
methodFrames.ask: "Identify and briefly explain two appropriate requirement elicitation techniques you would use." How many clauses per technique?

methodFrames.check: Four: who, what it collects, why it suits this project, and one limitation.
methodFrames.teach: 2024/2025 Question One (a), where the question itself asks for an advantage and a limitation. Answer in the shape the question names, in that order.
methodFrames.ask: Last one. "Create a use case diagram for the sports centre booking system." Which two things do most answers leave out?

methodFrames.check: The boundary rectangle, and the include and extend relationships.
methodFrames.teach: Actors outside the boundary, ovals inside it, include for what happens every time and extend for what happens only under a condition. Draw the box first, before any oval, and it cannot be forgotten.

lockin.big: "Read the ask, mark the scenario, run the recipe, validate, and write the steps as headings. The topic is new; the procedure never is."
lockin.sub: ERD five steps. DFD three levels and the balancing sentence. Use case four steps with the boundary drawn first. Read a diagram back in both directions. Requirements in four clauses.
